messages.subject: RE: error with jointprior function
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Sorry for the delayed response. I'm still struggling with the same problem. I understand that I can set a jointprior distribution to be uniform i.e. all possibilities are equally likely, in this case 0.25^813. But I'm still trying to figure out how to actually code this in R. Can anyone tell me how? 

If not then further questions to help me try and work it out myself. To try and understand what it is I need to create I went back to the ksl example described in the original deal paper (here: http://www.math.aau.dk/novo/deal/) and examined the output of the jointprior function for that example. I understand that the output is described in 6 parts jointalpha, jointnu, jointrho, jointmu, jointsigma jointphi and that these numbers are probability values for the different parts of the network (discrete, continuous etc) multiplied by the equivalent sample size N'. What I don't understand is how to interpret all the tables that are returned by jointprior. I've attached one example table for each of the 6 components. Would someone mind explaining them please? I've gathered that the different tables for the 6 components are for the different configurations of the variables. Two things are conf
 using me, what, in simple terms, are the numbers the probability of and why do only the diagonals have values other than zero? Secondly, what is the relationship between the rows and the columns of these tables, I see that the column/row names are the names of the variables but that's about all I get.

Wei, I realise you've already tried to answer this and I appreciate it, I'm just having a few conceptual problems. I don't have a maths background and this is all new to me. There are a couple of things in your previous reply that I can't follow. Specifically 'family(x_i)={x_i}\cup Parents(x_i)', I think this is roughly speaking 'the set of variables x_i that is not in the set Parents(x_i)' but I don't really know what \cup means. Second is the concept of equivalent sample size. deal talks about imaginary sample size, I assume this is the same thing but what is it. Is N' something that is calculated (and if so how?) or is it estimated and if so how do I know what is a sensible value?

Finally, can anybody recommend a good 'Introduction to Bayesian Networks' type book that breaks down the theory with good examples, I think I need to go back to basics.

Apologies for the length of this, I couldn't express what I need to know anymore concisely.
Thanks for your patience,
Richard
-----Original Message-----
From: wei luo [mailto:weiluosfu at yahoo.com]
Sent: Tue 8/1/2006 00:05
To: Richard Birnie
Subject: RE: [dealsoftware] error with jointprior function
 
Hi Richard,

Here is a thought, which may not be technically
correct. Please see (Heckerman 95) for notations.

When you do not have prior knowledge about parameters,
you may set 
p(x_1, x_2,...,x_813| B_sc^h)= 0.25^813,

then 
p(x_i = k, Parents(x_i) = j | B_sc^h) =
0.25^|family(x_i)|, 
where family(x_i)={x_i}\cup Parents(x_i) .

Then from the specified equivalent sample size N', the
quantities N'_ijk = N'*p(x_i = k , Parents(x_i) = j |
B_sc^h ) and N'_ij = \Sum_k{N'_ijk} can be caculated
for the current network, which defines Parents(x_i).
And the calculation of BDe score follows the equation
in Theorem 5. 

Note that here only N' needs to be specified, and
priors over parameters implicitly take symmetric
Dirichlet distributions.

Hope this helps.

Wei

2. Equivalent (imaginary) sample size can be
understood as the strength of your belief -- consider
empirical Bayes, where priors are from past
observations. 

I am in vacation right now; hope the brief explanation
still helps.

Cheers,

Wei

messages.subject: Bayesian network with time-series data...
messages.body_plain:
Hi. Dear all.

I'm doing some works to infer genetic networks by usign Bayesian 
network. And I have found "Deal" package written in R, and it is very 
easy to use.

At the moment, I have several time-series cDNA microarray data. As 
you might know, usually time-series data could be applied to "Dynamic 
Bayesian network" method. But in my understanding "Deal" doesn't have 
such functions and I'm not good at Matlab or the other packages where 
the 'Dynamic Bayesian Network' method is implemented and possible.

Of course, when I applied the time-series data into just "Bayesian 
Network", then I could have some good-looking results. But I'm not 
sure that would be quite significant and reliable. Moreover, my 
data's time points are only just 4!!!!. 

My main question is, in time-series data, what is the difference of 
results between using (normal) 'Bayesian' and 'Dynamic Bayesian' 
method. 

This is very basic and conceptual question, but I will really 
appreciate someone give me just a hint or clue.

Thank you in advance. Have a nice day...
